title: Garage door opener: safe teardown
summary: Take the ceiling head unit and rail of a garage door opener for its gear motor, transformer, remote receiver, infrared safety beams, light socket, backup battery and chain or belt. Never touch the door springs or cables: they can kill. Close the door, cut every power source including any backup battery, then clamp the door shut and lift the unit down with a helper.

steps.text: Look before you touch anything. This guide takes only the opener head unit on the ceiling and its rail. Find the door springs: a thick coil on a bar just above the door (torsion), or long springs beside the overhead tracks (extension), plus the steel cables from the bottom corners of the door. Leave all of them alone. If the opener is a wall-mounted box fixed to the end of the spring bar, leave it too.
steps.warn: Door springs, cables, drums and bottom brackets carry enough energy to kill. Never loosen, cut or adjust any of them. Read safety_garage_spring before you start.

steps.text: Close the door fully with the opener if it still has power, and keep the doorway clear. Do not clamp anything yet: cut the power in the next step first. If the door will not close, binds, sticks or jerks, a spring or cable may be failing: stop and leave the job. If the door is stuck open and there is no power, stop too: the opener may be what is holding it up.
steps.warn: Never stand or work under an open garage door, and never pull the release while it is open. A door with a weak or broken spring can drop with no warning.

steps.text: Take off rings, watches and loose clothing. Stand a stepladder on firm, level ground with a helper holding it (see step 6). Unplug the opener from its ceiling socket and keep the plug where you can see it. If it is wired in, switch off its breaker, tape it off and prove the supply dead with a meter (see safety_mains_isolation). If it has a backup battery, disconnect that too and tape its terminals.
steps.warn: Backup batteries keep the opener live with the mains off. Disconnect every power source before you touch it.

steps.text: Now clamp locking pliers or a C-clamp onto the track just above one roller so the door can't move. Check the door is fully closed. Then pull the emergency release cord to free the trolley from the opener, and pull the clip and pin where the door arm meets the bracket on the top of the door.
steps.warn: Only pull the release with the door fully closed. With the door open, a weak or broken spring can let it crash down.

steps.text: Disconnect the thin wires to the wall button and the two safety sensors at the terminals on the head unit. Label each pair with tape.
Set up a ladder under the head unit and a second ladder or a strong prop for your helper. Have the helper take the weight of the head unit before you undo anything holding it.
steps.warn: The head unit is heavy and awkward overhead. Never hold it alone on a ladder. Keep three points of contact, stay below the top two steps and don't lean out sideways.

steps.text: While the helper holds it, undo the bolts joining the head unit to its hanging brackets. Lower the motor end onto the top of the helper's ladder or prop.

At the door end, first support the front of the rail with a second helper, or a ladder or prop under it. Then pull the clip and pin joining the rail to the bracket above the door. Lower the rail end, then carry the head unit and rail down together, keeping the rail level.
steps.warn: The bracket above the door is often close to the torsion spring. Keep your hands, tools and the rail off the spring.

steps.text: Take the two safety sensors from low on each side of the door: unscrew them from their brackets and keep their wire. Take the wall button and its wire. Leave the bracket above the door on the wall.

On the bench, open the light lens and take out the bulb. If it is a compact fluorescent (the B970 allows them), unscrew it gently by its base and keep it whole: it holds mercury. If there is a backup battery, lift it out and tape its terminals. A sealed 12 V lead battery: follow safety_lead_acid. If the label says lithium, or the case is swollen, follow safety_swollen_lithium and do not open it.

Undo the cover screws and lift the cover off. Wait 5 minutes. Measure DC volts across the motor capacitor (a can on the motor of AC openers) and any large capacitors on the logic board. Discharge the motor capacitor, and anything else over about 30 V, with a resistor tool, then measure again: each must read under 1 V before you touch it (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: Some DC openers run their motor at about 140 V DC. Treat their boards like mains until you have measured them.

steps.text: Photograph the wiring. Unplug and unscrew the logic board (it holds the remote receiver), the transformer and the light socket. Keep the line cord.
Unbolt the motor and its gearbox from the chassis as one unit, with the worm gear, drive gear and output sprocket. Keep the limit switch or travel module with it. Leave the grease on the gears.
Back off the chain or belt tension nut, undo the master link, and slide the chain or belt and the trolley off the rail. Keep the rail, the sprockets and the idler pulley.
Test what you took: see Testing below. Don't power the motor straight from mains or a battery until you know what it is.

notes:
## Leave the springs alone

The springs carry nearly all the weight of the door. Chamberlain's manual says the door, its springs, cables, pulleys and brackets are all under extreme tension and must never be loosened or adjusted, and that the emergency release must only be pulled with the door closed, because a weak or broken spring can let an open door fall fast (Chamberlain B970). Follow safety_garage_spring and leave every spring, cable, drum, bottom bracket and the spring bar exactly as they are.

Wall-mounted openers fix to the end of the torsion bar with a collar and set screws, right beside the springs (Chamberlain RJO20). This guide does not cover taking them off. Leave them.

## What's worth keeping and why

- **Motor and gearbox.** A slow, strong gear motor: the motor turns a worm, which turns a drive gear and the output sprocket (Craftsman 139.53920D). Good for a winch (see build_motor_winch), a gate or a slow drive. The Craftsman 139.53920D runs on 120 V 60 Hz and its parts list has a 1/2 HP motor capacitor, which points to an AC motor that needs mains or a generator (Craftsman 139.53920D); check the motor label. DC units differ widely: the Genie 3022 runs a 140 V DC motor, while the LiftMaster 8500W wall unit has a 12 V DC motor with a 63:1 reduction (Genie 3022; LiftMaster 8500W). Read the motor label before you plan around it.
- **Transformer.** Steps mains down to low voltage inside the head unit; both Chamberlain parts lists include one (Chamberlain B970; Chamberlain RJO20). Useful for a low-voltage supply where mains exists. Test it with test_transformer.
- **Logic board with remote receiver.** Listens for remotes on 310, 315 or 390 MHz, depending on the brand and age (Craftsman 139.53920D; Genie 3022; LiftMaster 8500W). With its remotes and wall button it is a ready-made remote switch for a motor and a light. It will not run the door closed unless its safety sensors are connected and lined up (Chamberlain B970), so keep the sensors with it.
- **Safety sensors.** An infrared beam pair on a two-wire lead: the sender has an amber LED and the receiver a green one (Chamberlain B970). Keep them with their logic board to use as a beam across a doorway or path (see build_perimeter_alarm).
- **Light socket.** Usually a plain mains bulb socket, not an LED: the B970 takes an A19 incandescent bulb up to 100 W, and Chamberlain advises against LED bulbs because they can cut remote range (Chamberlain B970). Some take two bulbs (Genie 3022).
- **Backup battery** (newer openers). The B970's battery supplies 12 V DC, takes 24 hours to charge and lasts about 1 to 2 years (Chamberlain B970). The manual does not say what the battery is made of, so read the label: a sealed 12 V lead battery should be tested with test_lead_acid, a lithium one with test_lithium_cell, before you rely on it.
- **Rail, chain or belt, sprockets and trolley.** Steel rail for a sliding track; roller chain and sprockets for a pedal or wind drive; the idler pulley and trolley wheels. Also the line cord, bell wire and remotes, which take coin cells.

## Variations

- **Drive.** Chain (Craftsman 139.53920D; the Genie 3022 is sold as the ChainMax 1000) or toothed belt (Chamberlain B970); some makes use a long screw.
- **Motor.** AC with a capacitor on older units (Craftsman 139.53920D lists a 1/2 HP capacitor). DC on some units: the LiftMaster 8500W has a 12 V DC motor and the Genie 3022 a 140 V DC one (LiftMaster 8500W; Genie 3022). The Chamberlain B970 runs from a 12 V battery in an outage, but its manual does not say what its motor is (Chamberlain B970). Check the label: DC motor voltages range from 12 V to 140 V in the logged models.
- **Travel limits.** Older units use a gear-driven limit switch assembly plus an RPM sensor (Craftsman 139.53920D). Newer ones use an electronic travel module (Chamberlain B970).
- **Power.** Plugged into a ceiling socket, or wired in permanently through a hole in the top of the unit where local rules ask for it (Chamberlain B970).
- **Wall-mount openers.** Units such as the LiftMaster 8500W and Chamberlain RJO20 sit on the wall beside the door, and the RJO20 clamps onto the torsion bar (Chamberlain RJO20; LiftMaster 8500W). Leave them.

## What to leave

- **The springs, cables, drums, bottom brackets and torsion bar**, and anything bolted to the torsion bar.
- **The door and its tracks.** Leave the door closed and clamped until you are done. Before anyone uses the door by hand, follow safety_garage_spring: lift it slowly; a balanced door stays put halfway up (Chamberlain B970), and if it feels very heavy a spring has broken, so lower it gently and leave it.
- **The header bracket** above the door. It sits close to the spring and is only a small steel bracket.
- **The plastic cover and light lens.**

## Testing what you got out

- **Transformer.** Follow test_transformer: check the windings with the meter first, then measure the output on mains.
- **Motor.** Follow test_motor: check the windings for continuity with the meter, and test any capacitor with test_capacitor. Run an AC motor only with its own capacitor wired as it was.
- **Logic board and sensors.** Easiest to check before teardown if there is power: when the sensors are wired and lined up, the amber and green LEDs should glow steadily (Chamberlain B970).
- **Battery.** Read the label first. A sealed lead battery: follow test_lead_acid. A lithium one: follow test_lithium_cell.
